w: Founded in 1948, the philharmonic moved into a striking new building that went on to win the European Union Prize for Contemporary Architecture in 2015 - one of European architecture's most prestigious accolades, landing squarely on a concert hall in a mid-sized Polish port city.
s: Concert hall that won a top EU architecture prize
_facts: founded in 1948
in 2015, the new building was awarded the European Union Prize for Contemporary Architecture

w: At 6.9 kilometres, this avenue runs across Szczecin's west side through eight municipal neighbourhoods - and for years tourist brochures, and even the city's own website, called it the longest street in town. It isn't: Floriana Krygiera Street beats it by roughly 1.5 kilometres. The myth just won't quit.
s: The 'longest street in Szczecin' that actually isn't
_facts: length 6.9 km, runs through eight municipal neighbourhoods
press articles, brochures and even the city hall's official website have claimed it is the longest street in Szczecin
the actual longest street is Floriana Krygiera Street, about 8.5 km

w: Built 1725-1727 to a design by Gerhard Cornelius van Wallrawe, facade sculptures by Bartholome Damart, this Baroque gate once formed part of Szczecin's fortified walls, known first as the Berlin Gate, then the Brandenburg Gate. The walls came down in 1841; the gate stayed, hosting a community theatre today.
s: Baroque city gate reborn as a community theatre
_facts: historic Baroque city gate, built 1725-1727, designed by Gerhard Cornelius van Wallrawe, facade sculptures by Bartholome Damart
formerly known as the Berlin Gate and the Brandenburg Gate
part of the fortification walls until they were deconstructed in 1841
currently serves as a community theatre venue

w: Opened in 1911 on the Chrobry Embankment, this administrative building has outlasted the empire that built it, the war that followed, and the border that moved the city from Germany to Poland - still standing as the seat of the West Pomeranian Voivodeship Office today.
s: A 1911 office building that outlasted an empire
_facts: historic administrative building, opened 1911, located at the Chrobry Embankment

w: The oldest district in the city, sitting on the Oder's left bank where Stettin's story began. It carried the German name until 1950, when the city passed to Poland after the war - a small, quiet quarter today, population under 4,000, but the historical core everything else grew out from.
s: The historic core Stettin - now Szczecin - grew from
_facts: the core of the historic old German port city of Stettin until 1950
the oldest historical district in the city, on the left bank of the Oder
as of March 2021 had a population of 3,901

w: The largest humanities-focused library in West Pomerania, built around collections on Pomeranian, Scandinavian and German subjects, plus seamanship - a shelf list that quietly maps the region's tangled, border-crossing history. A general science reading room, covering mathematics and medical sciences, rounds it out.
s: A library shelving West Pomerania's tangled history
_facts: the largest humanities-oriented library in West Pomerania
focus on social sciences, Pomeranian, Scandinavian and German subjects and seamanship
also has a general scientific reading room covering mathematics and natural and medical sciences

w: A circular roundabout square developed in the 1880s, ringed by eclectic 19th-century tenements and a clutch of modernist apartment blocks dropped in during 1965. Five streets converge here, including the avenue named for Pope John Paul II - old Szczecin and postwar Szczecin sharing the same traffic circle.
s: 1880s roundabout ringed by tenements and modernism
_facts: a circular urban square forming a roundabout, developed in the 1880s
surrounded by historic eclectic-style tenements from the late 19th century and modernist apartment buildings from 1965
intersection of Pope John Paul II Avenue, Pilsudski Street, Rayski Street and Slaska Street

w: A quiet suburb on the Oder's right bank that hid something extraordinary in the 1930s: Dietrich Bonhoeffer's illegal seminary for the Confessing Church, run here from 1935 until outlawed in 1937. The war years brought a darker chapter: a forced-labour subcamp operating in the district under German occupation.
_facts: site of Dietrich Bonhoeffer's illegal (after 1937) Theological Seminary of the Confessing Church, 1935-1937
during WWII, Nazi Germany operated a forced labour subcamp of the Goleniow prison in the district

w: A tenement-lined mid-rise quarter developed through the 19th century that quietly holds a world record of sorts: Pionier 1907, one of the oldest cinemas anywhere still in continuous operation, running here since 1909. A slice of the West Pomeranian University of Technology campus sits within its boundaries too.
s: Home to one of the world's oldest running cinemas
_facts: mid-rise housing estate dominated by tenement houses, developed in the 19th century
within its boundaries lies the Pionier 1907, one of the oldest continuously operated cinemas in the world, dating to 1909
a portion of the West Pomeranian University of Technology campus is located there

w: Szczecin's most populous neighbourhood carries an outsized piece of history: the Central Cemetery, opened 1901, sprawls across 172 hectares here - over 300,000 burials, the largest cemetery in Poland, third-largest in Europe, among the largest anywhere. Traces of settlement go back to the Neolithic, long before that.
s: Poland's largest cemetery, 300,000 burials and counting
_facts: includes the Central Cemetery, over 300,000 burials, area of 172.33 ha, opened 1901
the largest cemetery in Poland, third largest in Europe, one of the largest in the world
most populous neighbourhood in Szczecin, 23,846 inhabitants in 2025
first signs of human presence date to the Neolithic period

w: A lakeside pocket of Szczecin on the eastern shore of Glebokie Lake, its single-family homes mostly dating to the 1930s and 60s. The lake's bathing-beach complex has drawn swimmers since the neighbourhood was folded into the city in 1939 - one of the quieter spots in Szczecin to actually get in the water.
s: Lakeside bathing beach folded into the city in 1939
_facts: located on the east coast of Glebokie Lake, area 31.4 ha, features a bathing beach complex
residential area with single-family detached homes dating mostly to the 1930s and 1960s
incorporated into the city in 1939

w: Once a cluster of upper-class villas built after 1871 on land sold off by Friedrich Carow, this district now holds the city's largest urban green space, Jan Kasprowicz Park, opened 1900, plus a Summer Theatre counted among the country's biggest amphitheatres.
s: Szczecin's biggest park, ringed by 19th-century villas
_facts: low-rise housing estate with historic villas, settled from the 14th century, sold in 1871 for development by owner Friedrich Carow
features Jan Kasprowicz Park, the largest urban green space in the city, opened 1900
Summer Theatre, one of the largest amphitheatres in the country

w: Two hamlets merged west of Szczecin's Old Town, home to one of the city's oldest buildings - a church in Krzekowo dating to the 13th century - and a monument to an unlikelier local legend: Wojtek, the Soldier Bear, who served alongside Polish troops and is remembered here with his own statue.
s: Home to a monument for Wojtek, the Soldier Bear
_facts: comprises Krzekowo and Bezrzecze, west of the Old Town
the church in Krzekowo is one of the oldest buildings in the city, dating back to the 13th century
there is a monument of Wojtek, the Soldier Bear, in Krzekowo
